result:
A race condition is when two or more processes touch the same resource at once and the result depends on who happens to get there first, so the output is correct most of the time and corrupted occasionally. With a shared log, the symptom is interleaved or lost lines when two scripts write at the same moment.

To avoid it, take a lock around the write with `flock`, and always append with `>>` rather than `>`:

```sh
{
    flock 9
    echo "$(date -Is) $$ job started" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/stockroom.log
```

The `flock 9` call blocks until no other process holds the lock on that file, and the lock is released when the block ends and descriptor 9 closes. Every writer has to use the same pattern, since the lock is advisory and does nothing against a script that ignores it.

For a single short line written by one `echo` or `printf`, `>>` alone is usually enough on a local filesystem, because the kernel appends each write as one unit. You need the lock when an entry spans several commands or lines, or when the file is on NFS.
